sentences.text: Iyuku was an iguanodontian dinosaur that lived in Africa during the Early Cretaceous period.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is an incomplete, semi-articulated skeleton featuring a partial skull, vertebrae, scapulae, pelvic girdle, legs, and ribs.
The genus name Iyuku derives from the Xhosa word for "hatchling," reflecting the immature nature of the known specimens.
Scientists discovered a unique bonebed containing at least 27 juvenile and hatchling individuals, a find never reported before.
Analysis of the bone tissue reveals rest lines, which indicate temporary growth arrests likely caused by environmental stress.
Fossils were recovered from the Kirkwood Formation in South Africa, dating to the Valanginian stage between 137.05 and 132.6 million years ago.
The fossils consist mostly of isolated bones of hatchlings and juveniles found in a 20 to 30 cm thick horizon without a preferred orientation.
Although no nests were found, researchers suggest the concentration of young individuals may represent seasonal mortality near a nesting site, with bones scattered by trampling or bioturbation.
Forster et al. (2022) noted similarities to juvenile remains of Orodromeus, Maiasaura, and Hypacrosaurus, suggesting possible mortality increases near nesting sites.
Bone histology reveals rest lines indicating temporary growth arrests, hypothesized to be caused by repeated environmental stress such as dry conditions or extreme heat.
The original describers assigned Iyuku to the Iguanodontia.
Later analyses by Poole (2022) recovered Iyuku as the sister taxon to Dysalotosaurus within the family Dryosauridae.

While no nests were found, researchers suggest the concentration of young individuals may represent seasonal mortality near a nesting site, with bones scattered by trampling or bioturbation, a view supported by similarities to juvenile remains of Orodromeus, Maiasaura, and Hypacrosaurus suggesting possible mortality increases near nesting sites.
